places.rationale: A long record of steady growth from a very low base and relative peace make improvement likely over 75 years, but very fast population growth, the repression around the 2025 election, rising water stress and low readiness to adapt leave a real tail of global-catastrophe or conflict-driven collapse.

The civil war since the 2021 coup has depressed today's baseline, so an eventual settlement inside a fast-growing region makes improvement the most likely outcome, but entrenched conflict, very low readiness to adapt and exposure of the Irrawaddy delta to cyclones and sea-level rise keep the downside large.

Today's baseline is already crushed by the SAF-RSF war and famine, so a lasting peace could lift living standards well above today's, but Sudan's near-permanent history of conflict, a debt of about 200% of GDP, extreme heat by 2100 and near-zero state capacity make prolonged collapse unusually likely.

Ample water, fertile land, new oil and a solid growth record favour improvement, while a population that may double, a heavy interest burden and an unresolved succession after Museveni are the main risks of conflict and stagnation.

A rentier state whose budget rests on oil and gas faces falling hydrocarbon demand and near-extreme water stress by 2050, so stagnation or a fiscal crisis is a serious risk, although its Saharan solar potential, cheap desalination and middle-income base leave room for improvement.

Iraq is caught between the shrinking flows of the Tigris and Euphrates under upstream dams and drought, heat that pushes the limits of habitability, a doubling population, and an oil-funded public payroll that the energy transition will squeeze, all under weak and militia-fragmented governance.

Isolation under the Taliban, women shut out of education and work, collapsing aid, mass returns from Iran and Pakistan, drought and very high fertility all weigh on prospects, although a baseline already depressed since 2021 and untapped mineral wealth give recovery a real chance over 75 years.

Yemen combines the weakest political stability in the set, a decade of war, aquifers close to exhaustion, dependence on imported food and energy, and a population still growing fast, so collapse is the largest risk here, even though recovery from today's war-wrecked baseline is possible.

Income per person has fallen since the 2014 oil bust, and an economy built on oil with poor diversification, the highest fertility in the set and a 25% interest burden make stagnation likely as oil demand fades, while relative peace limits the collapse tail.

Stable institutions, closeness to Europe, a world-class renewable resource, phosphate dominance and a growing manufacturing base favour improvement, and its severe and worsening water stress is being met with large-scale desalination.

Reforms since 2016, fast growth, peace and good health coverage favour improvement, while the main long-run threat is water: the Amu Darya and Syr Darya are under pressure from glacier loss past peak water, from upstream diversion such as Afghanistan's Qosh Tepa canal, and from heat.

An upper-middle-income country with effective government, low water stress and a role in the semiconductor and data-centre supply chains only needs modest growth to be better off and is best placed in this set for abundance, with ageing, the middle-income trap and conflict in the South China Sea as the main drags.

From one of the lowest living standards in the world, LNG and catch-up growth make a 25% gain likely, but the Cabo Delgado insurgency, post-election unrest, high debt, frequent strong cyclones and very low readiness to adapt keep conflict and collapse risks high.

Ghana has one of the steadiest democracies in Africa, near-universal electricity, low water stress and a diversified commodity base, so improvement is likely despite recurring debt crises and the damage illegal gold mining does to water.

Sound macro management and copper reserves that electrification will demand favour growth despite chronic political turnover and rising crime, while the loss of the Andean glaciers that supply the arid coast, El Nino and a large Lima earthquake are the physical risks.

Madagascar is one of the few countries poorer than at independence, and its recurrent coups (most recently in October 2025), 42% undernourishment, the weakest health coverage in the set, cyclones, southern drought and erosion make stagnation or worse unusually likely.

Rapid growth since 2012, ample water and new offshore oil and gas favour improvement, but a disputed fourth presidential term, unresolved succession, a recent civil war, jihadist spillover from the Sahel and the climate threat to the cocoa belt carry real risk.

Plentiful water and relatively good food security help, but the coming succession to a 92-year-old president, the Anglophone conflict, Boko Haram in the Far North and weak governance make a destabilising transition a major risk.

Steady poverty reduction, hydropower exports to India, near-universal electricity and low fertility favour improvement, while dependence on remittances, the political volatility shown by the 2025 Gen Z uprising, glacier loss with flood risk and a large overdue earthquake are the main hazards.

After the economy lost about three quarters of its size, today's baseline is so depressed that a political transition and partial return of the diaspora would likely lift living standards well above it, though oil reserves lose value as demand fades and governance remains among the weakest in the region.
